results.corrected_extracted: Acute toxicity data on nicotine are limited and come from three sources: animal studies, trials of nicotine as a medicine and poisoning reports. The animal studies do not adequately characterize acute toxicity; the medicine trials use amounts chosen, in part, because they are thought to be subtoxic; poisonings are documented, but it appears that the literature has not been assessed systematically for the relation between amount and effect; the commonly quoted human fatal oral amount is poorly documented (the chapter's literature search found no source for it). results.corrected_extracted: Inference about nicotine alone in pregnancy comes from studies comparing prenatal smokeless tobacco with prenatal smoking (smokeless products do not expose people to combustion products but all contain nicotine; Swedish snus has lower levels of certain toxicants than conventional smokeless products) and from randomized trials of nicotine therapy in pregnant women. Fetal growth: smokeless tobacco shows only modest contributions to lower birth weight; Swedish population study 1999 to 2010, snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.43), smaller than for smoking (the smoking figure is printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62 to 2.91, so it is not quoted); a trial of 250 pregnant women found no difference in quit rates or saliva cotinine between nicotine-patch and placebo arms but a birth weight 186 g higher (35 to 336) in the patch arm, possibly due to less smoking; the chapter reads these as supporting a modest role for nicotine in fetal growth restriction. Preterm delivery: smoking linked to a 27% higher risk (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited); rises of similar size with snus and with smoking in Sweden. Stillbirth: higher risk with smokeless tobacco in India and Sweden; in the Swedish study the smoking-related stillbirth risk fell markedly when antenatal bleeding and small-for-gestational-age deliveries were excluded while the snus risk stayed the same, which the chapter reads as both involving nicotine, with other factors possibly also contributing in smoking. Summary: the evidence supports the hypothesis that nicotine plays a key role in mediating the adverse effects of smoking on reproductive health, including preterm delivery and stillbirth.

results.corrected_extracted: Genotoxicity data are mixed (most studies negative; five positive: two for chromosomal aberration and sister chromatid exchange, and one each for micronuclei, an E. coli mutation assay and the Comet assay in nasal cells; DNA adducts also reported). Animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to be tumour-causing (one exception: sarcomas in one mouse strain); nicotine promotes tumours in some models but not those driven by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the animal findings do not support nicotine as a complete carcinogen. People: very little data; the Lung Health Study is the only source on long-term nicotine replacement (5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with replacement use; short follow-up); smokeless tobacco raises the risk of cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and pancreas (at least for some forms), less than smoking, and does not raise many smoking-related cancers, which suggests nicotine may not have a strong tumour-promoting effect, tempered by the different route (oral rather than inhaled). Summary: insufficient data to conclude that nicotine causes or contributes to cancer in humans; possible oral, oesophageal and pancreatic risks; substantial experimental evidence that nicotine is active in carcinogenic mechanisms; in vitro data suggestive but not supported overall by the most recent animal studies.

results.note: Paragraph ranges and nearly all statements match. Fixed: 'tend to' restored for the misclassification bias; source says 'no truly unexposed persons', not 'almost no'. Omits the report's case for pooling anyway (not pooling might leave conclusions more uncertain).
results.corrected_extracted: Random misclassification of exposure tends to reduce the apparent effect; classifying some people who currently or formerly smoked as people who never smoked would tend to push the lung cancer association upward when smoking clusters between spouses, but the analyses cited cannot fully explain the observed increase this way; because exposure has been widespread and almost unavoidable there are no truly unexposed persons, so estimates may be biased downward. Meta-analysis is used with the recognition that the uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what conventional statistics show, because of biases in or selection of the studies; one analysis of 37 studies suggested that smaller studies gave higher risks, another found little evidence of publication bias, and efforts to find possibly missing studies are said to have yielded little or nothing that would alter published conclusions (the printed sentence is garbled); the pooled results were not decisive for the causal conclusions. Confounding: adults with more exposure tend to have less healthful lifestyles in US and UK surveys (how far this generalizes is uncertain), socioeconomic status may lie on the causal pathway, and confounding matters more as associations get weaker.

In an INHANCE pooled analysis of 19 studies (13,935 cases and 18,691 controls), people who never smoked cigarettes but ever smoked cigars had an odds ratio of 2.54 (95% CI 1.93 to 3.34) for head and neck cancer, rising with frequency and duration, while the ratio was not raised among people who had ever smoked cigarettes.
